title: FOCUS: DLLMs Know How to Tame Their Compute Bound
one_liner: A diffusion language model can run faster by skipping the tokens it is not ready to decode yet, instead of wasting compute on impossible tokens.
lead: Diffusion language models (models that fill in words gradually, like painting a picture) decode differently than traditional models. Instead of one word at a time, they refine all words together in steps. But that makes them slow: at each step, the model computes predictions for all words, even though only some of them are ready to be picked. FOCUS fixes this by skipping the unreadable words and focusing work on the ones the model can actually use.

problem.h2: Diffusion models waste compute on impossible words
paras: A diffusion language model works in stages, like revealing words bit by bit. At stage one, all words are fuzzy guesses. By stage ten, most are clear. But at each stage, the model runs its compute on ALL words in the batch—even the ones still too fuzzy to decide on. Only some words are ready (confident enough to pick); the rest are just wasting compute cycles.

A beginner would try running the same compute on all words, hoping bigger hardware solves it. That fails because the hardware is already maxed out—the limit is not electricity, it is the time each word sits waiting to be decoded.

callout.html: Skip words that are not ready to decode yet; run compute only on the ones the model can use, and squeeze more words into the same time budget.

steps.text: Look at the focus weights (how much the model is focusing on each word) to rank which words are ready to decode.
Reorder the batch so decodable words come first; non-decodable words go to the back.
Run the model only on the front part (the ready words); skip the back part for now.
When a word is done, remove it from compute; when a fuzzy word gets ready, move it to the front.
By always running at full capacity on ready words, the system decodes more words per second.

paras: The paper changes which words get computed on at each decoding step. Instead of computing all words, FOCUS computes only the ready ones—using how much the model is focusing on each word to spot which words the model is confident about, and skipping the rest until they ripen.

hidden.name: Word importance from focus
paras: At each diffusion step, the model has an attention map (a set of weights showing how much it is focusing on each word). A high focus weight on word three means the model trusts its prediction for word three and is ready to decode it. A low weight means the word is still too fuzzy.

The paper measures this importance score directly from the model's own focus output. No extra computation; the signal is already there. The insight is that words with high focus (high importance) are the ones the model will actually decode in the next step—so the system should evict low-importance words and keep them off the GPU until they ripen.

heat.caption: Darker tokens have higher attention (readier to decode).

reads.html: The model's attention tells you which tokens it is about to decide on. Use that signal to predict which tokens will actually be decodable.
Attention-derived token importance scores correlate strongly with token-wise decoding probability, enabling dynamic computation reallocation.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: evict the unready to serve the ready faster
paras: Diffusion decoding is bottlenecked by how many words fit on the GPU at once. Each step, the model tries to decode many words in parallel, but only some are actually decodable. The rest sit idle, consuming memory and GPU time for nothing.

The paper's move is simple: evict the non-decodable words and pack more decodable words into the same GPU. The focus weights tell you which words are ready—the model is focused on that word, so it is ready to decode. The system reorders the batch to put ready words first, computes only on those, and leaves non-ready words in a buffer. When a word becomes ready, the system moves it to the front of the queue. When a word is done, it leaves. The result: the GPU is always at full capacity on words the model is actually ready to decode, so it decodes more words per second with the same hardware.

stages.s: Batch of all tokens, fuzzy and clear
Read attention weights to rank readiness
Sort: ready tokens to front, unready to back
Remove decoded tokens; move newly-ready tokens to front
More decoded words per unit time because GPU never idles

math.words: effective batch size (tokens computed) equals ready tokens at each step; throughput scales with the fraction of tokens ready times the batch size
symbols: fraction of tokens with attention weight above threshold
number of tokens in the batch

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Batch of 100 tokens. At step 5, attention weights say 35 tokens are ready (threshold: importance > 0.6).
Standard compute: run all 100 → 100 × cost = 1000 ops.
FOCUS compute: run only 35 ready → 35 × cost = 350 ops.

Same time per step; FOCUS finishes 350 ops while standard finishes 1000. But FOCUS can now fit more batches in the same wall-clock time: 1000 / 350 = 2.86× more batches, thus 2.86× throughput gain (the paper shows 3.52× in practice with better reuse).

math.note: By focusing compute on the ready tokens only, FOCUS packs more ready tokens into the same time budget, lifting throughput as if the batch size for useful work tripled.

items.html: If you mark a token ready when attention is still uncertain, you evict it too early and the decode fails. The threshold must be tuned per model.
Constantly sorting and moving tokens costs GPU time. If reordering is slow, the gains from compute savings vanish. Efficient reordering (via GPU sort) is critical.

If the model's attention weights do NOT predict which tokens will actually decode, the sorting hurts: you evict ready tokens by mistake. This only works if the model's focus aligns with decoding readiness.

Use the model's actual focus weights (no extra learned weights). Tune the threshold on validation data once per model architecture. Implement reordering as a fast parallel sort so it is faster than the compute savings it enables.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small diffusion language model (or use an existing one like DiffusionBERT). Run decoding on a large batch of sequences. Implement FOCUS: extract attention weights at each step, compute the importance score for each token, sort the batch to put high-importance tokens first, and skip compute on the rest. Measure tokens decoded per second (throughput) against the baseline (standard compute on all tokens).
demo.metric_eq: speedup = throughput_FOCUS / throughput_baseline; quality = task_accuracy_FOCUS minus task_accuracy_baseline
demo.closing: The demo must show that FOCUS decodes 2 to 3 and a half times more tokens per second without losing task accuracy.
